protein_diversity.notes: Outstanding protein variety — 5 distinct animal sources plus plant-based (chickpeas). Red meat, fish, poultry, eggs, and legumes all represented. Well distributed across the week.

vegetable_coverage.notes: Three dinners have abundant vegetables (shakshuka, kale Caesar, bronzino+kale), but Sunday and Tuesday are very low. The two kale nights help significantly. Lunches need to carry vegetables on low-veg days.

nutrient_gaps.detail: Zero dinners include whole grains — all starches are refined (hoagie roll, white pasta x2, corn tortillas). Lunches and snacks must compensate.
Only Wednesday (chickpeas, kale) and Friday (beans, kale) provide meaningful dinner fiber. Other nights are refined-carb heavy.
No fruit appears at any dinner — entirely normal, but lunches and snacks must provide 2-3 daily fruit servings.
Friday's bronzino and Thursday's mushrooms provide some vitamin D, but February sunshine is limited. Consider supplementation.

excesses.detail: Sunday (beef+cheese), Tuesday (butter+Parmigiano), and Saturday (cheese+crema) are all rich. Balanced by lighter Wed-Fri dinners.
Every dinner with a starch uses refined carbs. Not a crisis, but whole grain lunches would help balance blood sugar and fiber.

fiber_assessment.notes: Wednesday and Friday are fiber-rich; other nights are low. Weekly dinner fiber averages ~8g/dinner — below ideal. Whole grain lunches and fruit snacks are essential.

omega3_assessment.notes: Friday's bronzino provides omega-3 fatty acids. One fish dinner per week meets minimum recommendations. Add walnuts or flaxseed at breakfast for extra coverage.

weekly_assessment.overall_summary: This is a genuinely well-balanced dinner week with standout protein variety and some excellent nutrient-dense nights (Wednesday's kale Caesar and Friday's bronzino are nutritional powerhouses). The gaps — whole grains, fiber, and fruit — are entirely normal for dinner menus and easily filled through lunches and snacks. The heavier nights (Sunday, Tuesday) are balanced by lighter, vegetable-forward nights midweek. Valentine's week comfort food without nutritional guilt.

recommended_lunches.name: Whole Grain Turkey & Avocado Wrap
recommended_lunches.description: Whole wheat tortilla with sliced turkey, mashed avocado, shredded carrots, spinach, and a squeeze of lemon. Roll tightly and slice in half.
recommended_lunches.kid_notes: Elsie can help roll her own. Skip the spinach if she resists — the carrots and avocado carry the nutrition.

recommended_lunches.name: Lentil Soup with Crusty Bread
recommended_lunches.description: Red lentil soup with carrots, cumin, and lemon — make a big batch Sunday and portion for the week. Serve with a slice of whole grain bread.
recommended_lunches.kid_notes: Red lentils dissolve into a smooth, creamy soup that kids love. It doesn't look 'beany' — big win.

recommended_lunches.name: Mediterranean Grain Bowl
recommended_lunches.description: Quinoa or farro with cucumber, cherry tomatoes, olives, feta, and a lemon-olive oil dressing. Add rotisserie chicken for Dan's portion.
recommended_lunches.kid_notes: Let Elsie build her own with toppings she likes. Feta and olives are usually kid-winners.

recommended_lunches.name: PB&J on Whole Wheat + Fruit Side
recommended_lunches.description: Classic peanut butter and strawberry jam on whole wheat bread with a side of apple slices or clementines.
recommended_lunches.kid_notes: The eternal school lunch. Reliable, portable, and nutritionally solid with whole wheat.

recommended_lunches.name: Chicken Caesar Salad Wrap (Leftover Wednesday Dressing)
recommended_lunches.description: Use leftover Caesar dressing from Wednesday. Toss with romaine, grilled chicken strips, and Parmesan. Wrap in a whole wheat tortilla.
recommended_lunches.kid_notes: Kids who eat Caesar salad at dinner will eat it in a wrap at lunch. Smart leftover play.

recommended_lunches.name: Hummus & Veggie Plate with Pita
recommended_lunches.description: Hummus with carrot sticks, cucumber rounds, bell pepper strips, and whole wheat pita triangles. Add olives and cherry tomatoes for adults.
recommended_lunches.kid_notes: Most 8-year-olds love dipping. Hummus is a stealth nutrition vehicle — chickpeas, tahini, lemon.

recommended_snacks.name: Apple Slices with Almond Butter
recommended_snacks.description: Sliced Honeycrisp apple (use leftover apples from the Brussels sprout slaw) with 2 tbsp almond butter.

recommended_snacks.name: Greek Yogurt with Honey and Walnuts
recommended_snacks.description: Plain Greek yogurt with a drizzle of honey and a handful of toasted walnuts (save some from the pappardelle elevation).

recommended_snacks.name: Clementines (No Prep Required)
recommended_snacks.description: 2-3 clementines. That's it. Portable, mess-free, and bursting with vitamin C.

recommended_snacks.name: String Cheese + Whole Grain Crackers
recommended_snacks.description: 2 string cheese sticks with a handful of whole grain crackers. Zero thought required.

recommended_snacks.name: Trail Mix (DIY)
recommended_snacks.description: Mix almonds, dried cranberries (leftover from salad), dark chocolate chips, and pumpkin seeds (leftover from enchilada garnish). Bag in portions.

recommended_snacks.name: Banana with Peanut Butter
recommended_snacks.description: One banana, halved lengthwise, spread with peanut butter. Can freeze for a treat.

recommended_snacks.name: Pomegranate Seeds (Valentine's Snack)
recommended_snacks.description: A bowl of fresh pomegranate seeds — ruby-red for Valentine's week. Buy a container of pre-seeded arils to save time.

weekly_nutrition_summary: With these lunches and snacks supplementing the dinner menu, the family achieves solid coverage across all major nutrient categories. Whole grain gaps are filled by lunch wraps, pita, and crackers. Fruit intake jumps from zero (dinner-only) to 2-3 daily servings through snacks and lunch sides. Calcium coverage improves significantly with Greek yogurt, string cheese, and feta at lunch. The one remaining consideration is vitamin D — February in Virginia means limited sun exposure, and only two dinners (bronzino, mushrooms) provide meaningful vitamin D. A daily supplement of 600-1000 IU for all family members is a smart winter insurance policy.
special_notes: Consider a vitamin D supplement (600-1000 IU) for all family members during February — limited sunshine and indoor time make it hard to meet needs through food alone.
Elsie's swim lessons and YAT mean she's burning extra calories Tuesday and Friday — make sure she has a hearty after-school snack those days (trail mix + string cheese, or banana with PB).
Dan's Thursday potluck lunch will be heavy — the lighter mushroom pappardelle dinner is a good balance. He may want to go easy on snacks that afternoon.
The grocery list already includes walnuts, pecans, and chickpeas — repurpose leftovers into snacks to minimize waste and extra shopping.
